title: Introduction
content:
The problem A rule-based IDS such as Suricata is fast (well under a millisecond per packet) and almost never raises a false alarm on ordinary traffic — but it only sees what its rules describe. An attacker who encodes a payload a little differently, or who spreads an attack over many harmless-looking requests (directory scanning, password guessing), walks past it.
Large language models are good at reading a request the way a human analyst would. The question this project asks is:
Does an AI agent actually detect web attacks better than a rule-based IDS — where, and at what cost?
What the project builds Layer Component Role Target DVWA (+ MySQL) A deliberately vulnerable PHP application to attack Edge Nginx Reverse proxy; writes a JSON access log of every request Web firewall OWASP CRS on ModSecurity Industry-standard WAF, run in DetectionOnly mode as a baseline Network IDS Suricata Watches a copy of the traffic; ET Open + custom rules raise alerts Decision AI agent (LangGraph) Reads alerts + web log, asks the LLM, decides log / warn / block Model Ollama + Qwen2.5-14B Runs locally on an NVIDIA T4 GPU — no data leaves the machine Response ipset + iptables Blocks an attacker IP for one hour Visibility Flask dashboard Every decision with its reason, MITRE technique and analyst note Everything runs with Docker Compose on a single AWS EC2 g4dn.xlarge instance.
What it found (short version) On a test set of 147 requests (76 attacks, 71 benign), five runs per mode:
Mode Recall (attacks caught) False-positive rate F1 Suricata rules (rule_based) 0.32 0.00 0.48 OWASP CRS WAF (waf) 0.71 0.03 0.82 AI agent (agent) 0.95 0.10 0.93 The agent catches almost every attack, including encoded evasions and multi-request reconnaissance. It pays for that with more false alarms than the WAF or the IDS. An ablation shows the gain comes from reading the web log (seeing requests the IDS never alerted on), not from the LLM “re-thinking” IDS alerts. On 61 brand-new attacks never seen during tuning, the agent caught 61/61, the WAF 57, the IDS 35. The full numbers, with confidence intervals and what they do not prove, are in Results.
Who this guide is for Students or engineers who want to build a working IDS + LLM agent lab themselves. Anyone curious about how to measure an AI security tool honestly instead of showing a few cherry-picked demos. You will need some comfort with the Linux command line, Docker and basic AWS (launching an EC2 instance). No machine learning background is required.
This lab runs an intentionally vulnerable application. Deploy it only in an isolated environment and restrict every open port to your own IP address.

title: ECS Fargate Microservices
content:
This project implements a fully automated and secure microservices deployment platform on AWS, using ECS Fargate as the container orchestration engine and Terraform as the Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) tool. The goal is to build a production-ready architecture that is scalable, cost-optimized, and security-hardened, while enabling rapid and reliable application delivery through a complete CI/CD pipeline.
At the core of the system is an ECS Fargate service that runs containerized microservices. All AWS infrastructure components—including networking, security, compute, storage, and monitoring—are provisioned through Terraform modules. The project integrates AWS CodeBuild and AWS CodePipeline, allowing application updates to be automatically built, containerized, pushed to Amazon ECR, and deployed to ECS whenever new code is pushed to GitHub.
To balance security and cost, the system operates within private subnets without a NAT Gateway. Instead, it uses a collection of VPC Interface Endpoints (ECR, S3, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch, etc.) to allow ECS tasks to securely pull images and access required AWS services without exposing resources to the public internet.
Security is reinforced at multiple layers:
AWS WAF protects the Application Load Balancer (ALB) from common web exploits.
Amazon GuardDuty, VPC Flow Logs, and CloudWatch provide continuous threat detection and visibility.
Secrets Manager is used to store sensitive credentials such as database passwords.
Route 53 provides custom domain management and DNS routing.
This project demonstrates a modern, cloud-native, and production-aligned approach to running microservices on AWS—combining automation, observability, high availability, and strong security practices.
This this the architecture of the project:

title: VPC, Subnets, Security Groups
content:
The architecture consists of one VPC named ecs-fargate-microservices-vpc. Inside this VPC, 6 subnets and 4 security groups are configured to ensure that the application is secure and follows best practices
Public Subnets (for the Application Load Balancer) There are two public subnets, and they are used to host the Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Security Group for the ALB
Inbound rules:
Allow HTTP (port 80)
Allow HTTPS (port 443)
These ports allow users to access your website
Egress rules:
Only the required ports are allowed (in this case, port 3000) based on the least privilege principle This helps minimize risks such as:
Data exfiltration – containers sending data outside the network
Malware communication – connecting to malicious C2 servers
Lateral movement – accessing internal services that should be restricted
Compliance violations – breaking security standards Private Subnets (for ECS Tasks) There are two private subnets where ECS Fargate tasks run
Security Group for ECS Tasks
Inbound rules:
Only allow traffic from the public ALB security group on port 3000 (container’s application port) Egress rules:
Allow port 53 (DNS)
Allow port 443 (HTTPS)
Allow port 3000 (App)
Allow port 3306 (MySQl)
These are required for tasks to pull images, connect to AWS APIs, or resolve domain names
Private Subnets (for RDS Database) There are two additional private subnets dedicated for the RDS instance
Security Group for RDS
Inbound rules:
Only allow connections from the ECS task security group, using port 3306 (MySQL port) No outbound rules: the RDS database does not need internet access, so outbound traffic is blocked for security
Security Group for the VPC Endpoint (ECR Endpoint) This security group is attached to the Interface VPC Endpoint used by ECS tasks to pull container images from ECR privately (without internet)
Inbound rules
Allow HTTPS (443) from the ECS Task Security Group
This enables ECS tasks to access ECR through PrivateLink
Outbound rules
No outbound (egress) rule is required
Leaving egress empty is safe and follows strict least privilege best practice

title: Agent-IDS — Hybrid IDS + AI Agent
content:
Agent-IDS is a lab that puts an AI agent next to a classic intrusion detection system and measures, with numbers, whether the agent actually makes better decisions.
A vulnerable web application (DVWA) sits behind Nginx and an OWASP CRS WAF. Suricata watches the network traffic and raises alerts. An AI agent built with LangGraph reads those alerts and the web server’s access log, asks a local LLM (Qwen2.5-14B on Ollama, running on an AWS GPU) what each request is, and decides to log, warn or block the source IP. A dashboard shows every decision, and risky blocks can wait for a human to approve them.
The project then runs a controlled A/B experiment: the same 147 labeled requests are replayed against five decision modes (plain IDS, block-every-alert, WAF, the agent, and the agent limited to IDS alerts), five times each, and scored with confidence intervals.
This guide walks you through:
Introduction — what the project is and what it found How it works — the components, the decision graph and the life of a request Prerequisites — the AWS machine and tools you need Deploy the stack — from an empty GPU instance to a running system Try it — send attacks, watch decisions, approve blocks Run the benchmark — reproduce the experiment Results — the numbers and how to read them Errors and fixes — every problem hit while building it Notes and limitations — what to keep in mind Clean up — stop paying for the GPU

title: How It Works
content:
1. The big picture A request from a client goes Nginx → WAF → DVWA. Along the way, three logs are written:
Log Written by What it contains eve.json Suricata An alert when a packet matches a rule (signature, severity, source IP/port) access.json.log Nginx Every request: method, URI, body, status, request_id, source port audit.json WAF The CRS rules that matched, and whether the anomaly score crossed the blocking threshold The agent container polls these logs every 5 seconds. It runs with the host network so it can manage the host firewall.
2. Why read two sources? This is the key design idea.
Suricata produces high-signal alerts, but misses anything its rules do not describe (encoded payloads, single requests that are only suspicious as part of a series). The Nginx access log contains every request, including the ones Suricata stayed silent about. The agent reads both. When an alert and a web-log line describe the same request, they are joined into one event (by source port, method and URI) so the model sees the full picture once. Requests that only appear in the web log are still judged — that is where most of the agent’s extra catches come from.
To prove that, the benchmark also runs agent_ids: the same LLM and graph, but only Suricata alerts as input. It scores almost exactly like the plain IDS, which shows the gain comes from the data source, not from the model second- guessing alerts.
3. How the agent decides Each event goes through a LangGraph StateGraph:
triage — one LLM call per event. The model must answer in a strict JSON schema (enforced by Ollama’s grammar): reason — written first: the attack syntax it found, or the ordinary value it saw; action — block, warn or log; attack_type, confidence (= probability that it is an attack), mitre_technique, severity, analyst_note. route — if the model is unsure (confidence between 0.35 and 0.75), the event goes to investigate. investigate — a short ReAct loop (at most 3 steps) where the model may call read-only tools: recent alerts and web-log lines from the same IP in the last 15 minutes. Tools can only look; they can never block anything. risk_gate — a block with confidence below 0.90, or whose reason cites evidence that is not in the event (for example “IDS severity 1” when there was no alert), waits for a human. Unanswered items become warn after 15 minutes — the system never blocks without either high confidence or a person saying yes. act — the decision is written to SQLite; a block adds the IP to an ipset with a one-hour timeout. Why the reason comes before the action: with the reason written last, the model picked the action from surface clues (a page named fi “must be” file inclusion) and justified it afterwards. Making it state its evidence first removed six false positives on the test set.
Prompt-injection defense: request content is attacker-controlled text. It is wrapped in <<UNTRUSTED_DATA>> markers and the system prompt tells the model to treat anything inside as data, never as instructions. Tool output and memory lessons are fenced the same way.
4. The life of one attack request The attacker sends a request; Nginx and the WAF pass it to DVWA. The first request always gets through — the IDS only sees a copy of the traffic. Nginx writes the access-log line; Suricata matches a rule and writes an alert. Within 5 seconds the agent picks both up and joins them. The model answers in about 4.4 seconds. The IP is added to the block list. Every later packet from it is dropped. End to end this takes about 15 seconds (the MTTB — mean time to block — in the benchmark). 5. The five decision modes The same running stack can make decisions in five ways, selected with RESPONSE_MODE:
Mode How it decides Why it is there rule_based Suricata alert with severity ≤ 2 → block The classic IDS + auto-response naive Every Suricata alert → block A crude “block everything” baseline waf CRS anomaly threshold exceeded (rule 949110) → attack What most companies actually use for web attacks agent LLM graph, alerts + web log The proposed method agent_ids LLM graph, alerts only Ablation: separates “sees more” from “reasons better” 6. Optional: experience memory With MEMORY_ENABLED=true, the agent stores past decisions and the feedback it got (for example a human marking a block as a false positive). For a new event it retrieves the three most similar past cases (embeddings from nomic-embed-text) as examples. The benchmark measured whether this helps — it did not, measurably (see Results).

title: Application Load Balancer
content:
The architecture includes an Application Load Balancer (ALB) with a listener on port 80 and a target group with two IP-based targets
Listener (Port 80) Receives incoming HTTP requests from users
Forwards requests to the target group
Target Group (IP Targets) Contains two targets identified by IP addresses
Provides flexibility to register any network-accessible endpoint
Traffic flow: User → ALB (port 80) → Target Group → Targets (IP)

title: Prerequiste
content:
Follow the steps below to prepare your environment before deploying the infrastructure
Clone the project from GitHub Open your terminal and clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/nguyennt-fpt/ecs-fargate-microserviecs
Inside the project folder, you will find two main components:
getting-started-app/ – the source code used to build the Docker container ecs-project/ – the Infrastructure as Code (IaC) built with Terraform Install required tools Make sure the following tools are installed on your machine: Terraform, Git, AWS CLI, Docker Configure AWS CLI with an Access Key Step 1 — Create an Access Key
Log in to the AWS Console, navigate to IAM, select Users, choose the user you want to use, go to the Security credentials tab, click Create access key Follow the instructions then copy the: Access Key ID, Secret Access Key Step 2 — Configure a new AWS CLI profile
Open your terminal and run: aws configure –profile terraform
Enter the Access Key, Secret Access Key, region (e.g., ap-southeast-1), and output format
Step 3 — Set this profile as default
On Windows PowerShell or CMD: setx AWS_PROFILE “terraform”
Close the terminal and open it again so the environment variable takes effect Create an ECR repository You need an Amazon ECR repository to store your Docker image
In the AWS Console, search for ECR, click Create repository
Enter a repository name, click Create After creating it, open the repository and click View push commands.
Keep this window open — you will need those commands to push your image.
Build and push the Docker image Make sure Docker Desktop is installed and running
Open the folder: getting-started-app/
Open a terminal inside this folder
Paste and execute the push commands copied from ECR (These commands will log in to ECR, build the image, tag it, and push it) After completing the commands, go back to the ECR console.
You should now see an image inside your repository. Update the Terraform configuration Copy the repository URI from your ECR repository (Example: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/my-app)
Go to the folder: ecs-project/ then rename the file: terraform.tfvars.example → terraform.tfvars
Find the variable container_image and paste the repository URI with the latest tag:
container_image = “123456789012.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/my-app:latest”

title: Prerequisites
content:
1. An AWS GPU instance The model needs a GPU with about 10 GB of memory. The project uses:
Setting Value Instance type g4dn.xlarge (NVIDIA Tesla T4 16 GB, 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM) AMI Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (or the Deep Learning Base OSS Nvidia Driver GPU AMI, which has the driver preinstalled) Storage 50 GB gp3 (the model alone is ~9 GB) Region any region with g4dn capacity (the project used us-east-1) New AWS accounts often have a vCPU quota of 0 for G instances. Request an increase for “Running On-Demand G and VT instances” (at least 4 vCPUs) in Service Quotas before you start; approval can take a while.
Cost: an on-demand g4dn.xlarge is roughly 0.5 USD per hour in us-east-1. Stop the instance whenever you are not using it — a stopped instance only costs the disk.
2. Security group Open only what you need, and only to your own IP:
Inbound rules: SSH 22 <YOUR_IP>/32 HTTP 80 <YOUR_IP>/32 # DVWA through Nginx Custom 5000 <YOUR_IP>/32 # dashboard Outbound: all traffic (to pull images, rules and the model) Never open port 80 to 0.0.0.0/0. DVWA is vulnerable on purpose; anyone who reaches it can run commands on the box.
Home internet IPs change. If SSH suddenly times out, check that your current IP (curl https://checkip.amazonaws.com) is still the one in the security group.
3. An SSH key pair Create or choose a .pem key pair when launching the instance and keep it outside any git repository (or make sure *.pem is in .gitignore).
On Windows, the built-in OpenSSH may refuse the key with “UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE”. The ssh that ships with Git for Windows (Git Bash) does not have this problem.
4. Tools on your own machine Tool Used for Git cloning the project SSH client (Git Bash on Windows) connecting to the instance AWS CLI (optional) starting/stopping the instance from the terminal Python 3.10+ (optional) running the offline tests: python -m pytest tests -q 5. Source code git clone https://github.com/nguyennt-fpt/agent-ids.git Folder Content agent/ the LangGraph agent, prompts, tools (alert reader, firewall, memory) dashboard/ Flask dashboard ids/ Suricata config, custom rules, rule-update script webserver/ Nginx config benchmark/ corpus, replay, scoring, statistics, prompt-injection and learning-curve experiments tests/ offline pytest suite (no Docker or GPU needed) ops/ec2.sh start/stop helper for the lab instance

title: ECS Cluster
content:
On the AWS Console, when we view the ECS service, we can see a cluster The cluster has one service, which is currently running
This service is based on a task definition, which you can view in the Task Definition tab
The task definition specifies everything needed to run the containers, such as: ALB integration, desired number of tasks, auto scaling, rolling updates, etc In the Tasks section, you see the two running tasks. These are the two containers running the web app for this project
Here, the desired task count is set to 2, so ECS ensures that two tasks are always running

title: Provisioning Infrastructure
content:
Before you begin, make sure Terraform is installed on your machine
You can download and install it from the official website: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform
After installing, verify it using: terraform -v You now have all the necessary tools to start provisioning the infrastructure
Step 1: Open the project folder
Navigate to the ecs-project folder and open a terminal inside this directory Step 2: Run Terraform commands
You will use three main Terraform commands. Here is what each one does:
terraform init This command initializes the project It downloads the necessary providers (such as AWS) and prepares Terraform to run terraform plan This command shows you what Terraform will do before making any changes It generates a detailed execution plan so you can review all resources that will be created, modified, or removed terraform apply This command actually builds the infrastructure Terraform will ask you to confirm before proceeding. Once approved, it starts creating all the resources defined in your configuration files Step 3: Wait for deployment
The full provisioning process may take 15–20 minutes depending on the resources being created

title: Deploy the Stack
content:
All commands below run on the EC2 instance unless stated otherwise. Connect first:
ssh -i your-key.pem ubuntu@<EC2_PUBLIC_DNS> Step 1 — Install Docker (from Docker’s own repository) Ubuntu’s archive does not ship docker-compose-plugin, so use Docker’s official repository:
sudo apt-get update -y sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" | \ sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list sudo apt-get update -y sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin sudo usermod -aG docker $USER && newgrp docker Step 2 — NVIDIA driver and container toolkit Skip the driver part if you used the Deep Learning AMI.
# driver (plain Ubuntu AMI only), then reboot and SSH back in sudo apt-get install -y ubuntu-drivers-common sudo ubuntu-drivers autoinstall sudo reboot # NVIDIA Container Toolkit curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | \ sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list | \ sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' | \ sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list sudo apt-get update -y && sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-container-toolkit sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker sudo systemctl restart docker # check: you should see "Tesla T4" docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.0.0-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi Step 3 — Turn off automatic updates (recommended for a lab) Ubuntu’s apt-daily timers download and install packages in the background. In this project that broke two measurement runs (see Errors and fixes). Turn them off and update by hand instead:
sudo systemctl disable --now apt-daily.timer apt-daily-upgrade.timer # at the start of each work session: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y # reboot if NVIDIA, systemd or kernel packages were upgraded Step 4 — Get the code onto the instance git clone https://github.com/nguyennt-fpt/agent-ids.git ~/agent-ids cd ~/agent-ids Copying from a Windows machine instead? Use git -c core.autocrlf=false archive --format=tar HEAD | ssh ... 'tar -xf - -C ~/agent-ids'. A plain copy can turn every file into CRLF line endings and the shell scripts stop working.
Step 5 — Download the Suricata rules (ET Open) docker run --rm -v $(pwd)/ids/rules:/etc/suricata/rules jasonish/suricata:latest \ suricata-update --no-reload --disable-conf /etc/suricata/rules/disable.conf \ --output /etc/suricata/rules disable.conf turns off rules that cannot load in this lab (Modbus/DNP3) and a few noisy ones. Without it, suricata-update’s self-test fails and it silently keeps an empty rule file. Once the stack is running you can use bash ids/update_rules.sh, which also verifies the result and restarts Suricata.
Step 6 — Set the dashboard approval token (optional) The dashboard is read-only, except for one action: answering blocks that wait for a human. That action needs a token:
echo "APPROVAL_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 16)" > .env # .env is gitignored Without a token the approval buttons are disabled.
Step 7 — Start everything docker compose up -d docker exec ollama ollama pull qwen2.5:14b # ~9 GB, once docker exec ollama ollama pull nomic-embed-text # only needed for experience memory docker compose ps Expected:
NAME STATUS nginx running 0.0.0.0:80->80/tcp waf running dvwa running mysql running (healthy) suricata running ollama running (healthy) 0.0.0.0:11434->11434/tcp agent running dashboard running 0.0.0.0:5000->5000/tcp Check that Ollama really uses the GPU — this is the most common silent failure:
docker exec ollama nvidia-smi -L # must print "GPU 0: Tesla T4" Step 8 — Initialise DVWA Open http://<EC2_PUBLIC_IP>/setup.php and click Create / Reset Database. Log in with admin / password. DVWA Security → set the level to Low → Submit. The system is now running. Continue with Try it.

title: Resources
content:
Resources Created After Provisioning the Infrastructure with Terraform After running Terraform to set up the infrastructure, the following resources will be created:
VPC, Subnets, and Security Groups The foundational networking components that provide isolated networks, routing, and traffic filtering rules
Application Load Balancer (ALB) Distributes incoming traffic across ECS services to ensure high availability and scalability
ECS Cluster A container orchestration environment where your services will run on AWS Fargate
AWS WAF A web application firewall that helps protect applications from common web exploits
VPC Flow Logs and Amazon GuardDuty Security and monitoring services that analyze network traffic and detect suspicious or malicious activity
ECR VPC Endpoints Private endpoints allowing ECS tasks to pull container images from Amazon ECR securely without using the public internet
RDS and Secrets Manager A managed database instance and securely stored database credentials used by your application

title: Web Application Firewall
content:
The architecture includes an AWS Web Application Firewall (WAF) with several managed rules to protect the web application:
AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet (700 WCU) – protects against common web exploits such as XSS, path traversal, and other generic attacks
AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet (200 WCU) – specifically protects against SQL Injection (SQLi) attacks that try to manipulate your database queries
RateLimitRule – limits the number of requests from a single client within a time period to prevent abuse, brute-force attacks, or DDoS attempts
Together, these rules help the application filter malicious traffic, prevent common web vulnerabilities, and improve security and compliance
Note: Since the budget is limited, only basic managed rules are applied. If you want to enhance security, you can add additional WAF rules to cover more advanced threats

title: Try It
content:
1. Send a few attacks Get your DVWA session cookie from the browser (DevTools → Application → Cookies → PHPSESSID), then from your own machine run:
# SQL injection — write spaces as %20, not '+' curl "http://<EC2_IP>/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1'%20OR%201=1--&Submit=Submit" \ -b "security=low; PHPSESSID=<PHPSESSID>" # Reflected XSS curl "http://<EC2_IP>/vulnerabilities/xss_r/?name=%3Cscript%3Ealert%281%29%3C%2Fscript%3E" \ -b "security=low; PHPSESSID=<PHPSESSID>" # Command injection curl "http://<EC2_IP>/vulnerabilities/exec/" --data "ip=127.0.0.1;id&Submit=Submit" \ -b "security=low; PHPSESSID=<PHPSESSID>" # Path traversal / LFI curl "http://<EC2_IP>/vulnerabilities/fi/?page=../../../../../../etc/passwd" \ -b "security=low; PHPSESSID=<PHPSESSID>" And one ordinary request, to see the agent leave it alone:
curl "http://<EC2_IP>/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1&Submit=Submit" -b "security=low; PHPSESSID=<PHPSESSID>" With the default settings (BLOCK_ENABLED=true) the agent really blocks the IP it judges malicious — that is your IP. Port 80 will time out for an hour. SSH keeps working because only web traffic to the containers goes through the blocking rule. To unblock yourself:
docker exec agent python -c "from tools.firewall import unblock_ip; unblock_ip('<YOUR_IP>')"
To watch decisions without blocking, start the agent with BLOCK_ENABLED=false docker compose up -d --force-recreate --no-deps agent.
Testing on the instance itself? Use 127.0.0.1, not localhost. curl prefers IPv6 (::1) for localhost, and Suricata’s address variables are IPv4-only, so you would see no alerts at all.
2. Watch the decisions docker logs -f agent # one line per decision, with the reason docker exec suricata tail -f /var/log/suricata/fast.log # raw IDS alerts Open the dashboard at http://<EC2_IP>:5000. For each event you see the action, attack type, confidence, MITRE ATT&CK technique, severity, the model’s reason and an analyst note. A reason that does not match the evidence (for example it mentions an IDS alert that never fired) is marked ⚠ unverified.
3. See who is blocked docker exec agent python -c \ "from tools.firewall import get_blocked_ips; import json; print(json.dumps(get_blocked_ips(), indent=2))" docker exec agent ipset list agent-block # the kernel set, with the seconds left per IP Blocks expire by themselves after one hour, even if the agent restarts.
4. Approve a block yourself (human in the loop) By default high-risk blocks are auto-approved so the benchmark can run unattended. To make them wait for you:
AUTO_APPROVE=false HITL_ALL_BLOCKS=true docker compose up -d --force-recreate --no-deps agent Send an attack again. The decision now appears on the dashboard as pending, with three buttons (it asks for the APPROVAL_TOKEN you set during deployment):
Button Result Approve block the IP Warn record it as an attack but do not firewall Benign false positive → log (and, with memory on, a lesson for the agent) Prefer the terminal?
docker exec agent python approve.py # list pending items docker exec agent python approve.py <eid> approve # or warn / benign Nobody answers within HITL_TIMEOUT_S (15 minutes by default)? The item becomes warn — an unreviewed block never happens.
There is also a small interactive demo of the same gate:
docker exec -e AUTO_APPROVE=false -it agent python demo_hitl.py

title: Create https Protocal
content:
Enabling HTTPS for the Web Application
To enable HTTPS, you first need a hosted zone in Route 53, which requires a registered domain name. You can purchase a domain from any domain provider and point its nameservers to Route 53
Step 1: Create a Record in Route 53
Open Route 53 and go to your hosted zone
Click Create record
For Record type, select A – Routes traffic to an IPv4 address and some AWS resources
Under Route traffic to, select Alias to Application and Classic Load Balancer
Choose your existing ALB and click Create record
Now you can see a new record was created Step 2: Add an HTTPS Listener to the ALB
Go to the EC2 console → Load Balancing → select your ALB Click Add listener and choose Protocol: HTTPS
Select the target group (ecs-fargate-microservices-tg)
Under Default SSL/TLS certificate, click Request a new ACM certificate Copy the domain name from the record you created in Route 53 into the ACM domain name field
Leave other settings as default and click Create
Click Create record in Route 53 to validate the certificate A new record was created in Route 53 Wait approximately 2 minutes for the certificate to be issued Return to the Add listener page, select the newly created certificate, and click Create Step 3: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS
Select the listener on port 80 → Manage listener → Edit listener Choose Redirect to URL and set Port: 443, then save the rule Step 4: Test the Configuration

title: VPC Flow Log, GuardDuty
content:
The architecture also includes AWS GuardDuty and VPC Flow Logs to enhance security monitoring
AWS GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors your AWS accounts and workloads for malicious or unauthorized activity. It analyzes data from sources like VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail events, and DNS logs to detect threats such as compromised instances, reconnaissance activities, or unusual API calls
VPC Flow Logs capture information about the IP traffic going to and from network interfaces in your VPC. This allows you to monitor network activity, troubleshoot connectivity issues, and support security analysis by providing detailed traffic visibility
Together, GuardDuty and VPC Flow Logs help the project detect, investigate, and respond to potential security threats, improving overall cloud security

title: Run the Benchmark
content:
The benchmark is what turns this from a demo into an experiment. It answers “is the agent better?” with numbers that another person can reproduce.
1. The corpus benchmark/attack_corpus/corpus.jsonl holds 260 labeled HTTP requests, built by build_corpus.py from two data files:
Group What it is Why it is there clear_attack textbook SQLi, XSS, command injection, LFI, RFI the IDS should catch these evasion the same attacks, encoded or obfuscated where rules usually fail recon a directory scan and a password-guessing burst attacks spread over many requests benign_normal ordinary use of the same DVWA pages false-positive check fp_bait harmless text that contains attack keywords (“what is a UNION SELECT?”) the hardest false-positive check held_out 61 new attacks, never replayed while tuning a final, untouched recall test Payloads come from public sources (PayloadsAllTheThings, PortSwigger, OWASP, SecLists), not written by the author — so the corpus is not “built for the AI to win”.
The rows are split into dev (52 — tune the prompt here), test (147 — final numbers only) and held_out (61). Variants of the same technique always stay in the same split, so tuning on dev cannot leak test answers.
2. How one run works The agent container is recreated with the chosen RESPONSE_MODE and BLOCK_ENABLED=false (record, never block — otherwise the replay would block itself). replay.py sends the requests in a fixed order. Each carries a unique eid in its query string, and an actor IP in X-Forwarded-For so requests look like they come from different clients. score.py waits until every request has a decision (a slow run shows up as latency, never as “missed attacks”), then compares with the labels: block/warn = detected, log/no decision = benign. It writes Precision, Recall, F1, FPR, MTTB (mean time to block), p95 latency and per-group scores. run_ab.sh repeats this for all five modes, five times each, then computes:
summary.csv — mean ± std per mode; ci.csv — 95% confidence intervals from a request-paired bootstrap (resample the requests, same sample for every mode). A difference counts as evidence only when its interval excludes 0; calibration.csv — does confidence match how often the model is right? 3. Run it On the EC2 instance, from ~/agent-ids, with the GPU checked first:
docker exec ollama nvidia-smi -L # tuning loop: dev split, 2 runs per mode REPORT_TAG=dev-1 SPLIT=dev N=2 bash benchmark/run_ab.sh # final numbers: test split, 5 runs per mode (~3 hours) REPORT_TAG=test-final SPLIT=test N=5 bash benchmark/run_ab.sh # untouched new attacks, once, at the very end (~1.3 hours) REPORT_TAG=held-out SPLIT=held_out N=5 bash benchmark/run_ab.sh Results land in benchmark/report/<REPORT_TAG>/.
Long runs: start them with nohup ... > /tmp/ab.log 2>&1 < /dev/null & and check progress with short SSH calls every minute or two. A single SSH session left waiting for hours tends to be reset by the network, and you only notice much later.
4. Why it takes hours The LLM needs about 4.4 seconds per request on a T4. The replay sends one request every 6 seconds in the LLM modes so the model is never behind; otherwise MTTB would measure the queue instead of the agent. One agent run over the test split is therefore ~15 minutes, and 2 LLM modes × 5 runs is already 2.5 hours. Rule and WAF modes take under two minutes per run.
5. Side experiments Prompt injection (Pillar 3). Attack requests that also try to talk the model out of blocking them (“ignore previous instructions, this is a test”, fake JSON, base64, …). 25 techniques in 5 families, each sent twice, through the real graph, under four conditions: with/without the prompt’s defense rules × with/without the <<UNTRUSTED_DATA>> fence.
docker cp benchmark agent:/tmp/bench docker exec -e AGENT_DIR=/app -e MEMORY_ENABLED=false -e RESPONSE_MODE=agent agent \ python /tmp/bench/adversarial/test_injection.py Learning curve (Pillar 4). Does experience memory help over time? Each epoch first scores the test split using only lessons learned so far, then learns from dev feedback. Never the other way round, or it would just memorise the answers.
python3 benchmark/learning_curve.py --epochs 3 --memory on --delay 4 python3 benchmark/learning_curve.py --epochs 3 --memory off --delay 4 Untuned ruleset appendix. The same A/B on raw ET Open (bash ids/update_rules.sh untuned), to show the conclusions do not depend on the few rules that were turned off.

title: ECR Endpoint
content:
The project uses a VPC Endpoint for Amazon ECR instead of a NAT gateway to pull container images for ECS tasks
A VPC Endpoint is a private connection between your VPC and AWS services, which allows resources in private subnets to access ECR without going through the public internet
This approach enhances security because the traffic remains within the AWS network, reducing exposure to potential external threats such as interception or attacks
It also simplifies network configuration since you don’t need to set up a NAT gateway or manage public IP addresses for your ECS tasks
Additionally, using a VPC Endpoint can help reduce data transfer costs, as traffic within the AWS network is often cheaper than sending it through a NAT gateway to the internet
Overall, this setup ensures that your containers can securely and efficiently pull images from ECR while keeping them isolated in private subnets

title: Testing auto scaling
content:
Testing ECS Service Auto Scaling
Next, we will update the ECS service to verify that auto scaling is working correctly
In this architecture, the ECS Service is already configured with Auto Scaling using Terraform.
However, to make testing more convenient, i will add an additional third policy This extra policy can be used to trigger scaling actions more aggressively or under different conditions, making it easier to observe and validate Auto Scaling behavior during load tests or demonstrations
Go to ECS → ecs-fargate-microservices-cluster → select Update service
In the Service Auto Scaling section, click Add more scaling policy
Create a new scaling policy using the following settings:
Metric: ALBRequestCountPerTarget
Target value: 50
Scale-out cooldown: 60 seconds
Scale-in cooldown: 300 seconds
These values make it easier to trigger scaling events for testing purposes
To generate traffic, use a load-testing tool such as Apache Bench (ab) Run the command: ab -n 10000 -c 20 your-domain-name
-n 10000: total number of requests
-c 20: number of concurrent requests
After a short period, CloudWatch will detect increased load and trigger an alarm
Once the scaling policy activates, the number of running tasks will automatically increase
In this test, the service scaled from 2 tasks to 4 tasks
This confirms that the auto scaling configuration is working as expected

title: Results
content:
Final run: 2026-11-03, prompt v4, test split (147 requests: 76 attacks / 71 benign), 5 runs per mode. 95% confidence intervals in brackets. Raw CSVs: benchmark/results/.
1. Main table Mode Precision Recall F1 FPR MTTB rule_based (Suricata) 1.00 0.32 0.48 0.00 2.1 s waf (OWASP CRS) 0.96 0.71 0.82 0.03 2.6 s agent_ids (LLM, alerts only) 1.00 0.30 0.46 0.00 8.3 s agent (LLM, alerts + web log) 0.91 0.95 0.93 [0.88, 0.96] 0.10 [0.04, 0.18] 14.7 s agent, previous prompt v3 0.85 0.96 0.90 0.18 14.7 s naive (block every alert) gives exactly the same result as rule_based here.
Difference Recall FPR F1 agent − rule_based +0.63 [+0.52, +0.74] +0.10 [+0.04, +0.18] +0.45 [+0.33, +0.58] agent − waf +0.24 [+0.15, +0.34] +0.08 [+0.00, +0.16] +0.11 [+0.04, +0.19] 2. Where the agent wins and loses Group (caught / total, mean of 5 runs) n rule_based waf agent clear attack 26 13 23 26 evasion 26 7 23 26 recon 24 4 8 20 normal benign (false alarms) 42 0 0 5 fp_bait (false alarms) 29 0 2 2 On 61 new attacks (held_out): agent 61/61, WAF 57, Suricata 35. The WAF missed 3 remote file inclusions and 1 command injection; Suricata missed all 12 command injections. (Held_out contains only attacks, so false-alarm rates cannot be measured on it.)
3. How to read this The agent catches almost everything, including encoded evasions and reconnaissance — the kinds of attacks that slip past signatures. It still raises more false alarms (~7 of 71 benign requests) than the WAF (2) or Suricata (0). The original hypothesis “the agent reduces false positives” turned out to be wrong: on this data the IDS had none to reduce. The lead over the WAF comes from recon (20 vs 8): a scan or password-guessing burst is only suspicious as a sequence, and CRS has no rule for that. The data source matters more than the model. agent_ids — the same LLM fed only Suricata alerts — scores like the plain IDS. The extra catches come from reading the web log. The remaining false alarms are mostly logins with DVWA’s default accounts on the brute-force page. confidence is well calibrated (ECE 0.04); the MITRE technique is right for 85% of caught attacks. 4. Prompt v3 → v4 Prompt v4 makes the model write its evidence before its verdict and adds one worked example (“a plain page name is normal use; ../ is traversal”). It was chosen on the dev set against a criterion fixed in advance, before any test run. On test it removed the six fi/?page=<name>.php false alarms (FPR 0.18 → 0.10), at the cost of one new false alarm and one more missed directory-scan request. The two versions’ intervals still overlap, so treat the improvement as real on those cases but not yet firmly proven.
5. Side experiments Experiment Result Prompt injection, 25 techniques 0% bypass in all four conditions, even with every defense off. In the older run (12 techniques, prompt v2) 12% got through without defenses. The current set is too easy to show which defense matters. Experience memory, 3 epochs No measurable gain. Memory on: recall 0.95 → 0.92, FPR flat at 0.11. Memory off: recall 0.95, FPR 0.11 → 0.13. Differences of 1–2 requests. Untuned ET Open Same conclusions. Negative results are reported on purpose: an experiment that can only say “yes” is not an experiment.

title: RDS, Secret Manager
content:
When you search for RDS in the AWS Management Console, you can see that an RDS instance has already been created
To enhance security, the project uses AWS Secrets Manager to store the RDS credentials
By using Terraform, the RDS instance and its credentials are defined as code, which means sensitive information like database passwords is not hardcoded anywhere in the application or task definitions
Terraform provisions the RDS instance, the Secrets Manager secret, and links them automatically to ECS tasks or other applications
Secrets Manager can automatically rotate credentials, reducing the risk of compromised passwords
ECS tasks can securely retrieve credentials at runtime without exposing them
This approach ensures that your database credentials are protected, managed, and securely accessed, while keeping the infrastructure fully automated and reproducible

title: Errors and Fixes
content:
Every problem below actually happened while building and measuring this project. Each one is written as symptom → cause → fix, so you can search this page for the error you are looking at.
A. Infrastructure and deployment 1. Suricata sees no traffic at all
Symptom: no alerts, even for an obvious OR 1=1. Cause: the config listened on eth0, but EC2 Nitro instances name the interface ens5; local test traffic also goes over lo. Fix: set the right interface in ids/suricata.yaml (check with ip -br link), and keep HTTP_SERVERS: any. 2. curl localhost raises no alert
Cause: curl resolves localhost to IPv6 ::1; Suricata’s address variables are IPv4-only. Fix: use 127.0.0.1 or curl -4. 3. SQLi with + for spaces is not detected
Cause: the custom rule’s regular expression needs real whitespace after URL decoding; + is only a space in forms. Fix: write spaces as %20 when testing (a real rule weakness — an attacker could use it). 4. suricata-update “succeeds” but no ET Open rules load
Cause: 16 Modbus/DNP3 rules cannot load in this lab, so suricata-update’s self-test fails and it silently restores the previous (empty) rule file. Fix: --disable-conf ids/rules/disable.conf, and read the output for Suricata test failed. ids/update_rules.sh now stops with an error in that case. 5. Every DVWA page triggers an alert, even benign ones
Cause: ET rule 2221036 (HTTP response excessive header repetition) fires on DVWA’s own responses. Fix: disabled in disable.conf — the same tuning for every mode, and an appendix re-run on untuned rules. 6. Scripts fail on the server with $'\r': command not found
Cause: git archive on Windows with core.autocrlf=true exports CRLF line endings. Fix: git -c core.autocrlf=false archive .... 7. Re-deploying with tar fails with “Permission denied” in ids/
Cause: the Suricata container chowns files in its bind-mounted folder to its own user on every start. Fix: sudo chown -R ubuntu:ubuntu ~/agent-ids before extracting. 8. The agent hangs forever reading the Nginx log
Cause: the official Nginx image links access.log to /dev/stdout; opening it blocks. Fix: write the JSON log to a real file (access.json.log) and check os.path.isfile before reading. 9. Ollama container healthcheck always fails
Cause: the image has no curl. Fix: use ollama list as the healthcheck command. 10. Code changes do not take effect
Cause: the agent and dashboard code is baked into their images. Fix: docker compose up -d --build agent (and docker compose build dashboard). Config files that are bind-mounted (Nginx, Suricata) only need a restart. B. GPU and the host 11. Everything becomes very slow; ollama ps shows 100% CPU
Symptom: docker exec ollama nvidia-smi prints Failed to initialize NVML: Unknown Error. Cause: a known issue of the NVIDIA container toolkit with Docker’s systemd cgroup driver: a systemctl daemon-reload (for example after a package upgrade) can cut the container off from the GPU. Fix: docker compose restart ollama. Check docker exec ollama nvidia-smi -L before every measurement. 12. A benchmark run times out with 52 undecided requests
Cause: Ubuntu’s apt-daily timer ran during the benchmark. apt downloads over plain HTTP, Suricata alerted 211 times on apt’s user agent, and the agent spent ~12 minutes of GPU time triaging junk alerts while real requests queued. Fix: the noisy rule disabled; apt timers turned off (update by hand at session start); and duplicate alerts (same IP + rule within 5 minutes) are now judged only once. Lesson: an alert flood is also a way to slow the agent down. 13. After an automatic upgrade the GPU disappears completely
Symptom: Driver/library version mismatch on the host, Ollama cannot start. Cause: unattended-upgrades installed new NVIDIA libraries while the old driver was still loaded. Fix: let dpkg finish, then sudo reboot. Prevent it by turning off the apt timers (see 12). C. Measurement bugs (the dangerous kind — wrong numbers, no error) 14. Runs 2–5 of every mode scored recall 0
Cause: docker compose up -d does not recreate a container whose config did not change, so the agent’s memory of already-decided request ids survived between runs and it skipped everything. Fix: --force-recreate on every run. 15. The agent re-processed the previous run’s requests
Cause: at startup it read the last 100 lines of the Nginx log. Fix: start reading from the end of every log file, and track a byte offset afterwards. 16. Scoring started before the agent had finished
Cause: “no new decision for 15 seconds” was taken as “done”, but one LLM call can take longer. Fix: wait until every sent request has a decision (with a long safety timeout), and report undecided separately. 17. A truncated LLM answer marked a whole batch as benign (fail-open)
Fix: salvage every complete item from broken JSON, treat unknown actions as warn, give IDS events without a decision the rule-based verdict, retry web events twice, then warn. The system now fails closed. 18. Benign id=1 was flagged as SQLi
Cause: two artifacts of the benchmark itself: the random hex eid in the URL looked like an encoded payload, and in a batch the request was judged next to real SQLi on the same page. Fix: hide the eid from the model, and judge one event per LLM call (TRIAGE_BATCH=1). 19. IDS alerts contained other requests’ payloads
Cause: the replay reused one keep-alive HTTP connection for every simulated client, so one packet carried several requests. Fix: one connection per request. 20. False alarms grew from run to run
Cause: the investigate tools saw the same IP sending the same request in earlier runs and called it “repeated”. Fix: tools only look at the current run (since agent start, 15-minute window). 21. A calibration score that meant nothing
Cause: the scoring script read confidence as “how sure I am of my decision”, the model used it as “how likely this is an attack”. Nobody had defined it. Fix: define confidence = probability of attack in the schema and the prompt. Lesson: before an expensive run, check what every metric means, not just the headline ones. 22. The model wrote “IDS severity 1” when no IDS alert existed
Cause: the phrase was copied from an example in the prompt. Fix: removed from the examples, and a grounding check marks such reasons unverified and sends those blocks to a human. D. Working from Windows 23. ssh refuses the key: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE — use Git Bash’s ssh instead of the Windows one.
24. Remote commands lose their quotes in PowerShell — PowerShell 5.1 strips nested " when calling ssh.exe; use single quotes inside the remote command, or Git Bash.
25. A remote heredoc script stops silently halfway — a command inside ssh host 'bash -s' <<'EOF' that reads stdin (docker compose, scripts) swallows the rest of the script. Add < /dev/null to those commands.
26. SSH times out one day — your home IP changed; update the security group.

title: CICD
content:
Implementing CI/CD for Automated Build, Deployment, and Rolling Update
Now I will implement a CI/CD workflow so that whenever a developer pushes a new version of the application to GitHub, the code will be automatically built, the Docker image will be pushed to ECR, and the ECS service will perform a rolling update with zero downtime
Creating the CodeBuild Project Go to AWS CodeBuild and create a new project
Source provider: Select GitHub
If this is the first time connecting to GitHub, authorize the connection
Choose the repository that contains the application source code(In this case is getting-started-app)
For the webhook option, select: “Manually create a webhook for this repository in the GitHub console”
In the Buildspec section, select “Use a buildspec file”
Leave the filename empty because in the getting-started-app folder, there is already a file named buildspec.yml CodeBuild will automatically detect this file (If you use a different filename, enter the name here)
Copy the webhook URL provided by CodeBuild
Add webhook in GitHub, go to your GitHub repository → Settings → Webhooks, click Add webhook
Paste the webhook URL copied from CodeBuild, save the webhook
Ensuring IAM Permissions for CodeBuild Make sure that the CodeBuild service role contains the necessary permissions so it can:
Pull dependencies
Build Docker images
Push images to Amazon ECR
Interact with CloudWatch Logs
Interact with S3 (if artifacts are stored there)
Without these permissions, the build process will fail
Creating the CodePipeline Go to AWS CodePipeline and create a new pipeline
Choose “Build a custom pipeline”
For the Source stage:
Select GitHub
Choose the repository
Set Webhook event type = Push
For the Build stage:
Select AWS CodeBuild
Choose the CodeBuild project created earlier
For the Deploy stage:
Input artifact: choose the BuildArtifact
Deploy provider: Amazon ECS
Choose the ECS cluster and service that were created previously
Click Create to initialize the pipeline
Make sure the role of CodePipeline has permission to do the job
Testing the CI/CD Pipeline Now make a small change in the source code and push it to GitHub
Once the push is completed:
CodePipeline will automatically start running
The build stage will build the Docker image and push it to ECR
The deploy stage will update the ECS service
Observing the Rolling Update
After a short time, in the ECS service:
The number of running tasks increases to 4 (2 old tasks + 2 new tasks created for the rolling update)
After the new tasks pass health checks, ECS will terminate the 2 old tasks
This confirms that the rolling update worked correctly
Finally, visit the website again
The application now shows the updated version, meaning the CI/CD pipeline is functioning as expected
Navigate to ECR, there are a new image was push on the repository

title: Notes and Limitations
content:
1. Security notes Isolate the lab. DVWA is vulnerable on purpose. Restrict ports 22, 80 and 5000 to your own IP. Secrets stay out of git: the SSH key (*.pem) and .env (APPROVAL_TOKEN) are gitignored. Never print the token in logs or screenshots. The dashboard can change exactly one thing — the answer to a pending block — and only with the token. Any new write endpoint must be protected the same way. Tools are read-only. The model can look at logs but cannot block anything; only actions.py enforces decisions, after the risk gate. Blocks expire. IPs are added to an ipset with a one-hour timeout, removed by the kernel even if the agent crashes. Spoofed IPs: Suricata trusts X-Forwarded-For from every client (the replay needs it). An alert that cannot be joined with an Nginx line still carries the client-supplied IP, so the agent could block the wrong address. In production, trust that header only from your own proxy. 2. What the numbers do not prove Small scope: 147 test requests on one application. Real traffic contains far fewer attacks, so precision would be lower in practice. Payloads never execute: the replay does not log in to DVWA, so vulnerable pages redirect to the login page. Only detection on the request is measured; IDS rules that look at the response never get a chance to fire. The test set was used three times (three final runs as the prompt improved). v4 was tuned only on dev, but having seen earlier test results can still make the numbers slightly optimistic. Held_out is cleaner but contains only attacks, and is too easy (both prompt versions score 61/61). The prompt-injection set is too easy: with 0% bypass even without defenses, it cannot tell which defense helps. Throughput was not measured: the benchmark checks decision quality at one request every 6 seconds. 3. Would this work in production? Not as an inline filter on every request. One T4 handles about 15 requests per minute sequentially; a real website can receive hundreds per second. The realistic design is layered:
A WAF in the request path blocks known attacks instantly and cheaply. Only suspicious events (IDS alerts, WAF anomaly scores, unusual patterns) go to the LLM agent, which triages, investigates and writes a note for the analyst. Risky actions wait for a human. The agent’s ~15-second reaction time is fine for that role — a human SOC analyst takes minutes to hours — and it still stops multi-step attacks (scan → probe → exploit). Serving the model with a batching server such as vLLM, a bigger GPU, or a small model for first-pass filtering would raise throughput.
4. Lessons learned Measure at the decision layer with a unique id per request. It makes every number traceable to a request. Write down the success criterion before you look at the data, and keep a test set you do not tune on. Report negative results. Memory did not help; the injection set is too easy — both are useful findings. Most “model problems” were measurement problems. Batching order, a hex id in the URL and a copied example phrase caused more false alarms than the model’s reasoning did. The cheapest win was the data, not the model: adding the web log beat any prompt change.

title: Clean Up
content:
The GPU instance is the only expensive part. Choose how far you want to go:
1. Pause (keep everything for next time) On the instance:
docker compose down # stop the containers, keep the data and the downloaded model Then stop the instance in the EC2 console (Instance state → Stop), or from your machine:
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids <INSTANCE_ID> A g4dn takes 8–10 minutes to go from stopping to stopped. While stopped you only pay for the disk. When you start it again the public IP/DNS changes, and you should update packages by hand and check the GPU before measuring:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y docker compose up -d docker exec ollama nvidia-smi -L A safety net against forgetting: right after starting the instance, schedule an automatic shutdown, e.g. sudo shutdown -h +180 (3 hours). With the default “stop” shutdown behavior this stops the instance; it does not terminate it.
2. Reset the lab data docker compose down -v # also deletes MySQL data, logs, the decision DB and the Ollama model volume 3. Remove everything Terminate the EC2 instance (this deletes its root volume). Delete the security group and the key pair if you created them only for this lab. Delete any leftover EBS volumes or snapshots in the EC2 console.
